etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin compensatus, past participle of compensare (“to weight together one thing against another, balance, make good, later also shorten, spare”), from com- (“together”) + pensare (“to weight”).

definitions.definition: To do (something good) after (something bad) happens
To pay or reward someone in exchange for work done or some other consideration.

(transitive, intransitive) To make up for; to do something in place of something else; to correct, satisfy; to reach an agreement such that the scales are literally or (metaphorically) balanced; to equalize or make even.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “(please specify the page, or |century=I to X)”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The length of the night and the dews thereof do compensate the heat of the day.
The pleasures of life do not compensate the miseries.

definitions.definition: To adjust or adapt to a change, often a harm or deprivation.
